building.architect: Shea & Shea (Frank T. and Will D. Shea)

historical_record.description: The Saint Brigid parish, which later built this church, was founded by Archbishop Joseph Sadoc Alemany, who put it in the care of Dominican friars; its first territory ran from Bush Street north and from Larkin Street west to the ocean.
An earlier small wooden church stood on the site of the present sanctuary.
The Dominicans handed the parish and its earlier church to the diocesan clergy, two years after settling in the Western Addition.
The crypt, foundations and basement of the present church were built to plans by Shea and Shea, whose drawing showed a seven-story corner tower.
Saint Brigid Church, designed by architect Frank T. Shea.
After a pause in building, the superstructure was completed under Shea and Shea in the Richardsonian Romanesque style.

Roughly 90 percent of the walls are clad in recycled San Francisco granite curbstones and crossing stones, bought as streets were repaved and stored on the church lot; it was the city's first granite church.
The 1906 earthquake and fire damaged but did not destroy the granite church, which served as a refuge afterwards.
Repaired after the earthquake, the church was recommissioned on December 16, 1906.

A remodeling by architect Henry A. Minton added more seating and gave the church its Late Romanesque Revival front: he moved the narthex wall toward the street, built the four-story corner tower and designed the terra cotta ornament, made by Gladding McBean.
A building permit was taken out for remodeling designed by Henry A. Minton.
Low sacristies were added at the west end and new stained-glass windows by Harry Clarke Studios of Dublin were installed, with carpets from the Dun Emer Guild in Ireland.
The funeral Mass of Bank of America president Lawrence Mario Giannini, a parishioner, was held at the church.

A top story with a steep pyramid roof was added to the corner tower in darker granite, and the apse roof was raised and given a skylight; the rectory south of the church was demolished at about this time.
A three-manual, 85-rank organ built by Fratelli Ruffatti of Padua was installed in the rear gallery, completed in January 1983.
The Archdiocese of San Francisco closed the church.
The church was formally determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 252, Saint Brigid Church.

notable_residents.name: Rev. John E. Cottle
notable_residents.detail: The Rev. John E. Cottle, pastor for 37 years, planned the present granite church and collected the curbstones it is built of.
